{"filepath":"comparison_report.md","content":"# Comparison Report: Residential LFP (LiFePO4) vs Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries (VRFB)

Prepared: 10 September 2026
Contributors: Alice (research), Bob (research/data), Eve (warranty/O&M), Boss Dave (chair)
Inputs: lfp_battery_research.md; vanadium_flow_battery_research.md; team_discussion.md

Purpose
- Side-by-side, decision-oriented comparison for homeowners and integrators considering LFP (LiFePO4) vs vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB) for residential and small commercial use. This report synthesises prior research and the 10 Sep 2026 team discussion and highlights remaining uncertainties and next steps.

Executive summary and recommendation

Recommendation (short):
- For the vast majority of homeowners seeking daily cycling to maximize self-consumption, routine backup for outages of a few hours, or compact installations: choose an LFP-based home battery (LiFePO4). Rationale: higher system round-trip efficiency, compact footprint, mature supply chain, lower installation complexity and stronger availability of small-scale products and installers.
- For homeowners (or small commercial owners) whose primary objective is long-duration resilience (continuous backup or load shifting for 6–24+ hours, regular multi-hour discharge events, or a requirement for extremely high cycle endurance with low degradation): investigate VRFBs only if you can (a) accept substantially higher upfront installed cost per kWh, (b) have the space and installation tolerance for tanks/pumps, and (c) can procure a suitably sized system (often commercial-sized modules). VRFBs deliver long calendar life, very high cycle life, deep DoD and non-flammable electrolytes — but currently are less available in consumer-sized packages and typically cost more per usable kWh installed.

Best use cases at a glance
- LFP: daily self-consumption (solar shifting), compact backup (hours), EV + home integrated systems, constrained-space residences, installs requiring low-maintenance operations and simple warranties.
- VRFB: long-duration resilience and multi-day backup, sites requiring extremely high calendar/cycle life (many cycles/year over decades), installations where non-flammable electrolyte and chemical containment are preferred, and projects that can accept larger minimum sizes (hundreds of kWh) and professional O&M.

Side-by-side comparison (key metrics; normalised to usable kWh where relevant)

Notes on presentation: values are system-level, usable-kWh basis (team normalisation). Ranges reflect aggregated vendor datasheets and independent reports. Numbers explicitly flagged by the team as uncertain are marked [UNCERTAIN]. Confidence: High/Medium/Low indicates our judgement of provenance consistency across sources.

| Metric | LFP (LiFePO4) | Vanadium Redox Flow Battery (VRFB) | Notes & provenance / confidence |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Typical system round-trip efficiency (usable kWh basis) | 90% – 96% | 65% – 80% [UNCERTAIN] | LFP: vendor & system datasheets; system-level includes inverter/BMS losses (Confidence: High). VRFB: vendor/lab ranges 70–80% typical; lower values (65%) reported under some operating conditions; team flagged efficiency ranges as uncertain (Confidence: Medium).
| Usable DoD (practical) | 80% – 100% usable | ~80% – 100% usable | LFP often recommended 80–95% by vendors; VRFB electrochemically supports ~100% DoD (Confidence: High).
| Cycle life (to ~80% capacity at defined DoD) | ~3,000 – 10,000+ cycles (wide range by DoD) | >10,000 cycles (vendor claims 12k–25k+) | LFP cycle life depends on DoD and operating temp; VRFB vendors claim very high cycle endurance (Confidence: Medium).
| Calendar life / design life | Typical warranty 10 years; design life often 10–20 yrs | 15 – 30 years (vendor projections) | VRFB vendors commonly project longer calendar life; results depend on maintenance (Confidence: Medium).
| Installed cost ($/usable kWh) | ~$800 – $2,000 / kWh installed (marketwide range) [UNCERTAIN] | ~$1,000 – $2,500+ / kWh installed (small deployments) [UNCERTAIN] | Team flagged installed cost for both as highly uncertain for small residential installs; LFP pricing varies by region/scale/incentives; VRFB small-scale installed costs can be much higher due to minimum module sizes and BOS (Confidence: Low).
| Minimum commercially practical system size (typical) | 5 – 20 kWh consumer products widely available | Many vendors sell 100s kWh modules; true 10–20 kWh consumer VRFBs rare | VRFBs are commonly sold as larger C&I modules; small residential packages uncommon (Confidence: High).
| Energy density (pack/system) | Higher (smaller footprint per kWh) | Lower (larger footprint; tanks + pumps) | LFP: higher Wh/kg & Wh/L; VRFB: tanks/stack footprint increases site area (Confidence: High).
| Fire / thermal risk | Lower than many Li-ion chemistries; LFP has strong thermal stability | Very low (aqueous, non-flammable electrolyte) | VRFB advantage for fire safety; LFP still much safer than some other Li-ion chemistries (Confidence: High).
| O&M requirements (typical annual) | Low (inspections, firmware updates) | Higher (periodic electrolyte checks, pumps, membrane maintenance, O&M contract likely) | VRFB requires active O&M and periodic checks; LFP largely passive aside from monitoring (Confidence: Medium).
| Typical vendors (examples) | BYD, Pylontech, Tesla (Powerwall family historically), local OEMs | Invinity, Rongke, Sumitomo, various integrators | Vendor lists non-exhaustive; many LFP residential vendors and integrators exist; VRFB vendors primarily target C&I/utility (Confidence: High).

Detailed summaries

1) LFP (LiFePO4) — Summary for homeowners
- What it is: Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) is a lithium-ion cathode chemistry widely used in residential battery packs because it trades cell-level energy density for improved cycle life, thermal stability, and the absence of cobalt.
- System forms: Consumer products are available as packaged AC-coupled or DC-coupled systems (integrated inverter + battery or battery modules to hybrid inverters). Typical consumer module sizes: 5–20 kWh and up; systems commonly stacked for 10–40+ kWh.
- Performance highlights: high round-trip efficiency (90–96% system-level typical), deep usable DoD (80–100%), thousands of cycles depending on DoD and thermal management, and widely supported 10-year warranties (throughput limits vary by vendor).
- Safety & recycling: LFP has lower thermal runaway propensity than NMC; still requires proper BMS, enclosure, and local code compliance. Established recycling pathways exist but are still evolving for stationary LFP packs.
- Practical pros: compact footprint, broad installer ecosystem, off-the-shelf residential solutions, good for daily cycling and EV/home integration.
- Practical cons: finite cycle life vs flow chemistry (though high in absolute terms), potential for replacement within 10–20 years depending on use, fire-safety and recycling considerations.

Sources: lfp_battery_research.md; team_discussion.md


2) Vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB) — Summary for homeowners
- What it is: Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes circulated through an electrochemical cell stack; energy is (mostly) a function of electrolyte volume while power is a function of stack size. VRFB specifically uses vanadium electrolyte on both sides, which avoids cross-contamination issues.
- System forms: Commercial, modular systems with tanks, stacks, pumps and power electronics. Residential adaptation is possible but many vendors primarily sell modules at 100s of kWh and up; small consumer 10–20 kWh units are rare.
- Performance highlights: electrochemically can support near-100% DoD without serious capacity fade, vendors report very high cycle life (>10k cycles), and projected calendar life often 15–30 years with proper maintenance.
- Safety & handling: aqueous, non-flammable electrolyte reduces fire risk; however electrolytes can be corrosive and require spill containment and chemical-handling procedures.
- Practical pros: excellent longevity, decoupled scaling of energy/power, non-flammable electrolytes, well suited for long-duration storage and frequent deep cycling.
- Practical cons: larger footprint, lower round-trip efficiency (typical 65–80%), greater BOS complexity (pumps, tanks), limited small-scale products and potentially higher installed cost per usable kWh for small residential installs.

Sources: vanadium_flow_battery_research.md; team_discussion.md

Tradeoffs: concise discussion (cost, lifespan, efficiency, safety, installation)

- Cost (capex and installed): LFP benefits from larger manufacturing volumes and a mature residential supply chain; installed cost per usable kWh is generally lower for LFP at residential scale. VRFB deployed at small scale currently carries price premiums per usable kWh due to minimum module size, BOS, and less mature small-scale supply. Team flagged small-scale installed cost ranges as uncertain and requiring vendor quotes [UNCERTAIN].

- Lifespan & cycles: VRFBs claim higher cycle counts and longer calendar life if well maintained; this can lower lifetime replacement cost risk and be advantageous where many cycles per year are expected. LFP, while having a finite cycle life, can still deliver many years of useful service for typical residential use.

- Efficiency: LFP has materially higher round-trip efficiency (~90–96%), improving economics for daily cycling where energy arbitrage or self-consumption matters. VRFB efficiencies are lower (typical 65–80%), which penalises short-duration, frequent cycling use cases — the team noted the VRFB efficiency range as uncertain depending on system specifics [UNCERTAIN].

- Safety: VRFBs score strongly on fire safety (aqueous, non-flammable electrolyte). LFP is much safer than many other Li-ion chemistries but still requires electrical/fire safety measures and code compliance.

- Installation & footprint: LFP installs are compact and often easier to retrofit. VRFBs need space for electrolyte tanks and pumps and will often require a custom installation and stronger O&M relationship.

Recommended decision criteria for homeowners (checklist)

Ask these questions; use answers to guide technology choice:
1) What is my primary objective?
   - Daily solar self-consumption and bill savings -> LFP.
   - Short-duration outage backup (hours) -> LFP (smaller footprint & lower cost).
   - Long-duration resilience (6–24+ hours or multi-day) -> VRFB may be appropriate if you can accept larger footprint and cost.
2) How many kWh do I actually need? (usable kWh target)
   - Typical self-consumption home: 5–15 kWh will cover many households; LFP products are available across this range.
   - If you need 50–200+ kWh of usable energy for multi-day resilience, VRFB modular scaling is attractive — but check minimum module sizes and installed cost per usable kWh (team flagged small-scale VRFB pricing as uncertain).
3) What space is available? If space is tight (garage/basement), LFP is likely the better fit.
4) Am I willing to contract for O&M / chemical handling? VRFBs typically require an O&M agreement and periodic maintenance; LFP systems usually require less active maintenance.
5) What is my budget and payback horizon? LFP generally has lower upfront installed cost per usable kWh today for residential sizes. Where lifecycle economics matter (very high cycles/year and long life), VRFB may be competitive — but run LCOS with vendor quotes.
6) Do local codes or building insurers prefer non-flammable electrolytes? If so, VRFB may reduce permitting friction.

Sizing guidance (3–6 kW PV household examples)
- Objective: maximise same-day PV self-consumption (daily cycling)
  - Typical recommended LFP system: 6–12 kWh usable (1–2x daily household evening load). LFP preferred for compact size and efficiency.
- Objective: backup for single-night outage (6–12 hours for modest loads)
  - LFP: 12–24 kWh usable depending on load profile and critical circuits.
- Objective: multi-day resilience (24+ hours)
  - VRFB logical choice for large requirements; practical residential VRFB deployments often start at 100s kWh due to module sizing and may be cost-prohibitive for small homeowners. If multi-day resilience is required, get firm vendor quotes and O&M terms.

Note: these sizing rules are heuristics. The team agreed on normalising to usable kWh and running LCOS scenarios with vendor quotes for firm procurement decisions.

Open questions and uncertainties (action items & owners from team meeting)
- Installed cost per usable kWh for representative LFP and VRFB products in our local market (include BOS & installation). Owner: Alice. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026. Status: outstanding [UNCERTAIN].
- System-level round-trip efficiency measurements (installed systems) for candidate products; independent test reports vs vendor claims. Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026. Status: outstanding [UNCERTAIN].
- Warranty texts, throughput caps and conditional clauses for shortlisted products (legalised warranty excerpts). Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026. Status: outstanding.
- O&M annual cost estimates for VRFBs (pump maintenance, electrolyte checks, consumables) vs LFP (inspection, monitoring). Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
- Minimum practical residential VRFB system size and any suppliers offering small (10–50 kWh) packaged products. Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
- LCOS model runs for three target use cases (daily cycling, 6–12 h backup, 24+ h resilience), with sensitivity to round-trip efficiency, installed cost, and cycle life. Owner: Boss Dave. Deadline: 24 Sep 2026.

Consolidated references and sources (selected)

Primary internal artifacts used in this report
- lfp_battery_research.md (Alice, 10 Sep 2026)
- vanadium_flow_battery_research.md (Alice, 10 Sep 2026)
- team_discussion.md (Meeting notes, 10 Sep 2026)

External / vendor & technical references (representative links)
- Invinity Energy Systems (VRFB vendor): https://www.invinity.com
- Rongke Power (VRFB manufacturer): https://www.rongkepower.com
- Sumitomo Electric (flow battery materials / products): https://global-sei.com or https://sumitomoelectric.com
- PNNL Flow Battery overview & research (US Dept. of Energy national lab): https://www.pnnl.gov
- DOE / US Energy Storage and Redox Flow overview pages (historical reports): https://www.energy.gov/eere/vehicles/energy-storage
- Wikipedia: Vanadium redox flow battery: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanadium_redox_flow_battery
- Wikipedia: Lithium iron phosphate battery: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_iron_phosphate_battery
- Tesla Energy (Powerwall product pages & specs): https://www.tesla.com/energy
- Example residential LFP vendors (BYD / Pylontech / other OEMs): https://en.byd.com; https://www.pylontech.com.cn

(Notes: the above external links are representative starting points; where vendor datasheets or independent test reports are used they will be collected for the next team meeting.)

Appendix: flagged numbers & rationale
- Installed costs for small residential VRFBs and per-usable-kWh installed cost for both chemistries were explicitly called out in the meeting as data gaps and should be treated as uncertain in procurement decisions. These items are marked [UNCERTAIN] in the main tables.
- VRFB round-trip efficiency range was discussed in the meeting and flagged as sensitive to stack design, operating power/current density and balance-of-plant decisions; team requested independent system-level efficiency tests before procurement. Marked [UNCERTAIN].

Next steps and recommended immediate actions
1) Collect vendor datasheets and itemised installed quotes (usable kWh basis) for shortlisted LFP and VRFB products (Owner: Alice; deadline 17 Sep 2026).
2) Gather independent system-level performance reports (efficiency & aging) for shortlisted products (Owner: Bob; deadline 17 Sep 2026).
3) Obtain warranty/legal text and sample O&M contracts for shortlisted units (Owner: Eve; deadline 17 Sep 2026).
4) Run LCOS model scenarios (Owner: Boss Dave; deadline 24 Sep 2026) once vendor quotes are available.

Prepared for: internal use by the project team and for sharing with procurement stakeholders and homeowner advisors; not a substitute for vendor-specific due diligence and local code/permitting checks.

Recorded by: Alice (compilation), verified against team_discussion.md
